name: Dahlia Purple
lede: Dahlia Purple is a dark purplish red named for the dahlia flower, carried over from Ridgway's 1886 Nomenclature of Colors and also recorded among traditional Japanese names as Ebizome, "vine grape."

sections.title: A flower, and a Japanese grape
sections.body:
Ridgway carried Dahlia Purple over from his 1886 *Nomenclature of Colors* into his fuller 1912 standard, where it sits on plate XII, hue 67, tone k; Maerz and Paul date the name to that same 1886 origin [1]. The ISCC-NBS dictionary of 1955 filed the name under block 260, very dark purplish red, though by measurement the swatch sits only 2.3 units from the centroid of block 259, dark purplish red [2]. Its nearest named neighbors in our library are [[old-mauve|Old Mauve]] at 2.7 units and [[velasquez|Velasquez]] at 3.0 [2].

Our data also carries a Japanese traditional name for the same swatch, Ebizome (蒲萄), meaning vine grape, after the dark skin of wild grapes rather than the dahlia flower that gives the English name [3]. [[byzantium|Byzantium]], 7.3 units off, is the nearest of the everyday names [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of Dahlia Purple covers at least five per cent of the canvas in only 5 of them, as photographed [4]. The earliest is Jacopo Bassano's *Adoration of the Magi*, from 1568 [4]. It is a dark, specific color that rarely covers enough of an aged, varnished canvas to register at our threshold, so its scarcity here says little either way about how often painters used it [4].

origin.source: Ridgway, Color Standards and Color Nomenclature; Maerz and Paul, A Dictionary of Color; ColorHub library
